design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42021226447) of observational studies comparing higher- with lower-potency cannabis, as each study defined potency, for psychosis or psychosis-like symptoms, anxiety, depression and cannabis use disorder. MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO from inception to 14 January 2021, plus reference lists. 20 articles met the criteria; by the editors' count they report 16 distinct studies (the GAP case-control study in four articles, EU-GEI in two): 2 case-control studies, 1 prospective cohort, 9 cross-sectional studies (one of them in people using medical cannabis) and 4 naturalistic or repeated-measures studies in people using medical cannabis. Narrative synthesis by outcome; risk of bias with a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.
can_establish: Which observational studies up to January 2021 compared higher- with lower-potency cannabis on psychosis, anxiety, depression and cannabis use disorder, in which designs and samples, how the reviewers rated their quality, and the direction and adjusted size of each study's association as the review reports it.
cannot_establish: A pooled size of any association (no meta-analysis was possible), whether higher potency causes any of these outcomes (all studies observational, most cross-sectional, potency taken from what people said they used), the THC dose people actually took, or much about concentrates, which were studied only in four cross-sectional samples and one small clinical sample.

sample.recruitment: Database search of MEDLINE (from 1 January 1966), Embase (from 1 January 1974) and PsycINFO (from 1597), all to 14 January 2021, with terms for cannabis, potency and the four outcomes, no date or language limits but English terms only, and reference lists of identified articles (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st paragraph, p. 736). The included studies sampled patients with first-episode psychosis and local population controls (UK; 17 catchment areas in England, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain and Brazil), patients followed after psychosis onset (UK), respondents to online drug surveys (20 countries, n = 181,870; 175 countries, n = 55,240; UK, n = 2,514), a UK sample of 1,087 people aged about 24 with childhood measures, US convenience samples (156, 191 and 574 people), 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders, and people using medical cannabis in the Netherlands, Canada and the US (Tables 1 to 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: observational studies of humans with quantitative data on cannabis potency as a direct or indirect comparison of higher- with lower-potency products (as each study defined them, so read in relative terms), quantitative data on symptoms, diagnosis or relapse of depression, anxiety, psychosis, or cannabis use disorder, dependence or misuse, and an association between the two. Excluded: conference abstracts, editorials, correspondence, and experimental studies (Methods, 2nd paragraph, pp. 736-737). At full text 69 of 89 articles were excluded: 44 conference abstracts, editorials or correspondence, 10 not observational, 7 without lower-potency cannabis as the comparator, 6 without higher-potency cannabis as the exposure, 2 without an outcome of interest (Figure, p. 737).
sample.demographics: Mean ages in the included samples range from 24 years (UK online survey; UK sample of 1,087) to 52.8 years (Dutch medical cannabis study); women make up 16.9% (Japanese patients) to 53% (EU-GEI controls; one Canadian medical sample). Countries, by the editors' count of the 16 studies: UK 4, US 5, Canada 2, the Netherlands 1, Japan 1, multinational 3 (Tables 1 to 4).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition in the one cohort is not reported in the review.
sample.selection_effects: Three databases with English terms; no grey literature, registries or experts; conference abstracts excluded; the search ended in January 2021 and the review was published online in July 2022. Most included samples are self-selected (online drug surveys with pictorial aids, US convenience samples, people using medical cannabis) or clinical (first-episode psychosis, cannabis-related disorders). The review's senior author is an author of at least five included studies and another review author is first author of one (see funding); no procedure for selecting or appraising the authors' own studies is described.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in every study (with pictorial aids in the online surveys and an optional photo upload in one US study): product type (skunk or sinsemilla against hash, grass or resin; butane hash oil or concentrates against herbal cannabis; liquid or resin against dry herbal cannabis) or a stated THC band (typically 10% or more against under 10%; labelled percentages in the medical cannabis studies). No included study measured THC in the cannabis people used or THC intake; the authors call the exposure a highly simplified measure of THC content (Discussion, 5th paragraph, p. 748).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency of use was adjusted for in some studies, combined with potency into one variable in others (for example daily use of higher-potency cannabis) and not considered in others; amount used was adjusted for in only one study (the 175-country survey); route was not analysed (Discussion, 8th paragraph, p. 748; Tables 1 to 4). Strength bands are study definitions only.
exposure.polysubstance: Only as each study adjusted: tobacco, alcohol and other drugs in the two case-control studies; alcohol, other illicit drugs and cigarettes in the cohort; other substance use in the 20-country survey; tobacco added to cannabis in the 175-country survey; no adjustment listed in four smaller cross-sectional studies (Tables 1 to 4).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; exposure windows ranged from current use or the past 12 months to lifetime use and were not specified in several studies (Tables 1 to 4).

comparison.controls: Lower-potency cannabis as each study defined it (hash-type, grass or resin, herbal cannabis, under 10% THC, dry herbal), or never-use of cannabis in the two case-control studies and former use in the cohort, in which case the comparison of higher with lower potency is indirect (Discussion, 6th paragraph, p. 748).
comparison.matching: EU-GEI controls were sampled to represent the catchment population by age, gender and ethnicity, and GAP controls came from the same area (Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs, p. 740); no matching in the other studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Reasons for choosing stronger products (the authors name self-medication by people with poorer mental health as possible reverse causation), earlier mental health outside a few studies, family history and socio-economic position outside one UK sample; the authors state there is no agreement on which confounders matter (Discussion, 8th paragraph, p. 748).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Adjusted in the case-control studies, the cohort and two surveys; not in the smaller US and Japanese samples (Tables 1 to 4).

outcomes.instruments: Psychosis: first-episode psychosis by the Schedules for Clinical Assessment in Neuropsychiatry or ICD-10, relapse as psychiatric admission, self-reported lifetime diagnosis, the DSM-5 cross-cutting symptom measure, ICD-10 clinical interview, a semi-structured interview or a self-report scale for psychosis-like experiences. Cannabis use disorder: Severity of Dependence Scale (two online surveys; 0 to 15, cut-off 3 or more), Cannabis Abuse Screening Test (UK sample), MINI cannabis screening test (US sample of 191), a self-report questionnaire (US sample of 156), ICD-10 clinical interview (Japanese patients). Anxiety and depression: self-reported lifetime diagnosis, the Clinical Interview Schedule-revised, the DSM-5 cross-cutting measure, a mental-health self-report scale, and visual analogue or symptom scales in the medical cannabis studies (Tables 1 to 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: Two reviewers rated each study independently on a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and categorised it as good, fair or poor (details in appendix p 6, not read). None was rated good: by the editors' count of Tables 1 to 4, 5 of the 16 distinct studies were rated fair (the two case-control studies, the cohort, the UK sample of 1,087 and one Dutch medical cannabis study) and 11 poor, with scores from 0 to 8; the same study could score differently by outcome.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Higher' and 'lower' potency are relative within each study: the authors state that the exposure can be read only in relative terms within a study, not in absolute terms across studies (Discussion, 6th paragraph, p. 748).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four outcome domains, with more than 50 study-level estimates printed across Tables 1 to 4 (editors' count); the review gives no rule for when a set of findings counts as consistent.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening, full-text selection, extraction and risk-of-bias rating were done by two reviewers independently, with disagreements resolved with the senior author (Methods; Contributors, p. 749).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Study-level estimates as the review prints them (odds ratios with 95% CI unless stated). Psychosis: GAP (UK) skunk-type use against never-use 2.91 (1.52 to 3.60), hash-type 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77), daily skunk-type 5.40 (2.80 to 11.30), earlier onset hazard ratio 1.68 (1.08 to 2.63); EU-GEI types of 10% THC or more against never-use 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2), under 10% 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5), daily 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3) and 2.2 (1.4 to 3.6), positive symptoms 0.22 (0.02 to 0.29) against 0.09 (-0.12 to 0.28); relapse cohort 3.28 (1.22 to 9.18) against 1.82 (0.36 to 8.75); 20-country survey higher- against lower-potency herbal 1.28 (1.07 to 1.53), butane hash oil against lower-potency herbal 1.11 (0.85 to 1.46); US sample of 156 concentrates r 0.11 (-0.20 to 0.40), higher-potency herbal -0.27 (-0.45 to -0.06); Japanese patients 0.212 (0.061 to 0.735); psychosis-like experiences 1.29 (0.67 to 2.50) and Cohen's d 0.12 (fewer with concentrates). Cannabis use disorder: Severity of Dependence Scale b 0.254 (0.161 to 0.357) per extra day a month of higher-potency use, grass 0.020 (-0.029 to 0.070), resin 0.025 (-0.019 to 0.067); b 0.155 (0.100 to 0.209) and 0.262 (0.188 to 0.337) for the higher-potency classes in the 175-country survey; recent problems 4.08 (1.41 to 11.81); dependence syndrome 6.850 (1.866 to 25.145); US sample of 156 r 0.09 (-0.12 to 0.30) and -0.05 (printed -0.35 to -0.26); US sample of 191 means 2.1 against 1.3, not significant. Anxiety: generalised anxiety disorder 1.92 (1.11 to 3.32); butane hash oil 1.80 (1.60 to 2.01) and 1.72 (1.55 to 1.91); higher- against lower-potency herbal 1.05 (0.98 to 1.12); US samples null. Depression: 1.18 (1.11 to 1.25), butane hash oil 1.34 (1.21 to 1.48) and 1.15 (1.03 to 1.25); major depression 1.28 (0.68 to 2.32); US samples null. Medical cannabis studies: varied, several without intervals or statistical tests.
analysis.covariates: None at review level; estimates were extracted from each study's fully adjusted model, with covariates listed per study in Tables 1 to 4.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42021226447, described as prospectively registered (Methods, 3rd paragraph, p. 737); PRISMA followed. The registry record was not read, so planned and reported analyses could not be compared; the paper explains why no meta-analysis was done (Discussion, 7th paragraph, p. 748).
analysis.selective_reporting: All four outcomes are reported, with the medical cannabis studies separated. Several estimates are printed without intervals ('95% CI NS'), and several numbers differ between the text and the tables (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not applicable; no pooling. Several included samples are small (71, 102, 156 and 191 people).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Psychosis: in two case-control studies and one cohort, all rated fair, stronger cannabis (skunk-type, or types of 10% THC or more) was associated with first-episode psychosis compared with never-use (adjusted odds ratios 2.91 and 1.6; 5.40 and 4.8 with daily use) while lower-potency use was not (0.83; 1.1), although daily lower-potency use was in EU-GEI (2.2); continued daily use of stronger cannabis was associated with relapse (3.28) and stronger cannabis with earlier onset (hazard ratio 1.68). Cross-sectional findings for psychosis were mixed, including no association for concentrates in two samples and an inverse one in a clinical sample. Cannabis use disorder: four of six cross-sectional studies (one fair, three poor) found more dependence severity, problems or dependence with higher potency, and the two comparing concentrates with herbal cannabis found no significant difference. Anxiety: one fair study and the butane hash oil comparison in one large survey found associations, others did not. Depression: small associations in one large survey only. No study was rated good, and none measured THC.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Abstract says higher-potency use "was associated with an increased risk of psychosis and CUD" and that evidence varied for depression and anxiety, which matches the results. Gaps: (1) the Discussion calls the association with cannabis use disorder consistent, but two of the six studies found no significant association and all six were cross-sectional, five rated poor; (2) 'risk' wording comes from mostly cross-sectional data, which the authors themselves say cannot establish direction; (3) the Conclusion draws recommendations for education, clinical management and THC-based regulation without a certainty rating of the evidence; (4) the psychosis evidence concerns skunk-type cannabis or types of 10% THC or more, not concentrates as a separate form, while the Introduction motivates the review with concentrated extracts, and the studies of concentrates themselves were few, cross-sectional and mostly null; (5) several printed numbers disagree between text and tables. Against this, the Discussion is explicit about self-reported exposure, proxies, reverse causation, the lack of agreement on confounders and why no meta-analysis was possible, and argues that titration would bias associations toward the null.

timeline.event: First GAP article (Di Forti et al., 2009): in a preliminary analysis of 454, patients with first-episode psychosis more often used higher-potency cannabis than controls (as summarised in this review).
Full GAP sample (Di Forti et al., 2015) and a UK online survey of potency and dependence severity (Freeman & Winstock, 2015), both included here.
UK cohort of relapse after a first episode of psychosis (Schoeler et al., 2016), the only prospective cohort included.
20-country online survey of butane hash oil (Chan et al., 2017), the largest included sample and the main source on concentrates.
EU-GEI case-control study across six countries (Di Forti et al., 2019), described by the review as replicating GAP; it shares its first author with the GAP articles.
Meta-analysis of the prevalence of cannabis use disorder among people who use cannabis, cited in this review's Introduction for its 22% estimate
This review: the first systematic review of cannabis potency and mental health and addiction, by its authors' account.
Narrative review of flower, concentrates and edibles and cannabis use disorder (online 2024, issue 2026), which does not cite this review

replication.where_it_stands: The only systematic review on this question read for the encyclopedia. It pools nothing, so its weight is that of its studies: the psychosis conclusion rests on two case-control studies sharing a first author and one cohort, all rated fair; the cannabis use disorder conclusion rests on six cross-sectional studies, three of the four positive ones co-authored by the review's senior author. Claims must count the GAP study's four articles and EU-GEI's two articles once each, must not count the review's own authors' surveys as independent of the review, and should quote numbers from the tables, which differ from the text in places.

funding.funder: KP: South West Doctoral Training Partnership studentship funded by the Economic and Social Research Council. GT: Cancer Research UK Population Researcher Postdoctoral Fellowship (C56067/A21330) and Cancer Research UK project award (PPRCPJT\100023). LH: Wellcome Trust (209158/Z/17/Z). The funder had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing (Acknowledgments, p. 749).
funding.declared_conflicts: GT reports previous funding from Pfizer (GRANT scheme) and owns a scientific consulting company doing work unrelated to this project; KP, SO, LH, SA and TPF declare no competing interests (Declaration of interests, p. 749).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Universities of Bath, Bristol and Birmingham and University College London. The reference list shows the senior author (T P Freeman) as an author of at least five included studies (EU-GEI 2019, Freeman & Winstock 2015, Chan et al. 2017, Hines et al. 2020 and Craft et al. 2020) and L Hines as first author of Hines et al. 2020; these supply the fair-quality anxiety and cannabis use disorder findings, three of the four positive cannabis use disorder findings and the main concentrate data. The review also recommends measurement tools (the iCannToolkit and the standard THC unit) developed with its authors' involvement. No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry funding or ties are printed. Recorded as reasons to read closely, not to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts of people who use cannabis, recruited before problems begin, that record the products used and THC exposure (tested or labelled content in standard THC units, with frequency and amount), measure cannabis use disorder and psychosis by diagnostic interview over years, adjust for earlier mental health and reasons for use, and are run by groups other than those that produced most current studies; for concentrates, the same design in places where they are widely sold.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Observational human studies; exposure higher-potency cannabis; comparator lower-potency cannabis, both as each study defined them; outcomes depression, anxiety, psychosis and cannabis use disorder (Methods, 2nd paragraph, pp. 736-737).

Described as prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD42021226447) and done to PRISMA (Methods, 1st and 3rd paragraphs). The registry record was not read, and the paper does not say whether a meta-analysis was planned or whether anything changed from the protocol.
Experimental studies were excluded for a stated reason: the authors wanted real-world exposure to the potency and amount used (Methods, 2nd paragraph).

Three databases from inception to 14 January 2021 with key terms given and the strategy in the appendix, plus reference lists, and no formal date or language limit; but English search terms only and the exclusion of conference abstracts, editorials and correspondence (44 of the 69 full-text exclusions) are not justified, and no grey literature, registries or experts were searched. Judged as AMSTAR 2 item 4 is written, as for the batch 3 cards; the senior author decides the project's reading of this item (decision p-amstar2-item4).
KP and SO screened titles, titles and abstracts, and full texts independently (agreement 96.2%, 89.9% and 89.9%), with disagreements resolved with TPF (Methods, 3rd paragraph; Contributors).
KP and SO extracted independently into a spreadsheet, cross-checked by KP (Data analysis; Contributors).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The flowchart gives reasons for the 69 full-text exclusions as counts, and the text says the specific exclusions are reported in appendix p 5, which was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 1 to 4 give for each study the design, location and years, participants with sample size, age and sex, exposure and comparator, how exposure was collected, the timing of exposure and outcome, the outcome measure, the confounders adjusted for, the main findings and the quality score.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale was applied by two reviewers independently per outcome, covering selection, comparability (confounding) and exposure and outcome measurement; the modifications and domain scores are in appendix p 6 (not read); selective reporting of results is not assessed, and the summary into good, fair or poor hides which domain failed in which study, although the text names the main shortfalls.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported for any included study.
No meta-analysis; the reasons are given (self-reported exposure, no precise measure of THC exposure, differing definitions of higher and lower potency; Discussion, 7th paragraph).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion states that no study was rated good and discusses self-reported exposure, product type as a proxy, titration, cross-sectional designs and confounding (5th to 9th paragraphs). The Conclusion and the sentence calling the cannabis use disorder association consistent do not carry these limits through.

Differences in how studies defined higher and lower potency, and in direct against indirect comparisons, are discussed as the reason results can be read only within studies and could not be pooled (Discussion, 6th and 7th paragraphs); inconsistent findings are partly explained (few symptoms in one sample, low rates of psychosis and a self-reported outcome in another, a small clinical sample).
No meta-analysis; publication bias is not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and author interests are declared (p. 749); the paper does not flag that its authors wrote several included studies.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can be judged only from appendix p 5, which was not read. One critical item fails (item 4: English search terms and the exclusion of conference abstracts without justification, no grey literature, registries or experts), which gives low confidence; if item 7 also failed the rating would be critically low. Items 2 and 9 are partly met and item 13 is met; items 11, 12 and 15 do not apply because nothing was pooled. The review is registered, screened, extracted and appraised in duplicate and describes its studies in full tables; the main weakness for readers lies in its evidence rather than its conduct: no study rated good, mostly cross-sectional designs, self-reported potency, and a Discussion sentence calling the cannabis use disorder association consistent when two of six studies found none. Cite it for which studies exist and what each found as reported, preferring the tables where text and tables differ.

key_findings.finding: MEDLINE (from 1966), Embase (from 1974) and PsycINFO (from 1597) were searched to 14 January 2021 with English terms for cannabis, potency and the four outcomes (no date or language limits), plus reference lists. 6,389 records, 2,218 duplicates, 4,171 titles screened, 89 full texts assessed and 69 excluded (44 conference abstracts, editorials or correspondence; 10 not observational; 7 without lower-potency cannabis as comparator; 6 without higher-potency cannabis as exposure; 2 without an outcome of interest), leaving 20. Two reviewers screened and assessed independently (agreement 96.2%, 89.9% and 89.9%).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Figure (PRISMA flowchart, p. 737)

key_findings.finding: 20 articles, printed as 20 studies with 119,581 participants: 8 on psychosis or psychosis-like symptoms, 8 on anxiety, 7 on depression and 6 on cannabis use disorder. By the editors' count the tables hold 16 distinct studies (the GAP study in four articles, EU-GEI in two): 2 case-control, 1 prospective cohort, 9 cross-sectional (one in people using medical cannabis) and 4 naturalistic or repeated-measures studies in people using medical cannabis. None was rated good; 5 were rated fair and 11 poor (editors' count from the risk-of-bias column).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Tables 1 to 4 (risk-of-bias column)
key_findings.note: The printed participant total is smaller than the sample of one included survey (181,870); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: GAP case-control study (UK, 2005-10; 410 patients with first-episode psychosis and 370 controls from the same area; rated fair): in a preliminary analysis of 454, patients more often used higher-potency cannabis than controls (adjusted odds ratio 6.8, 95% CI 2.6 to 25.4); in the full sample of 780, skunk-type use against never-use 2.91 (1.52 to 3.60), hash-type 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77), daily skunk-type use 5.40 (2.80 to 11.30), with daily lower-potency use not associated. EU-GEI case-control study (17 catchment areas in England, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain and Brazil, 2010-15; 901 patients and 1,237 population controls; rated fair): types of 10% THC or more against never-use 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2) after adjustment for daily use, under 10% 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5); daily use 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3) for higher and 2.2 (1.4 to 3.6) for lower potency. Both adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, education, employment, tobacco, alcohol and other drugs.

Earlier onset of psychosis by about 4 years with higher-potency use (hazard ratio 1.68, 1.08 to 2.63; GAP, adjusted for gender and frequency). Positive symptoms in 901 first-episode patients: higher-potency use against no use 0.22 (0.02 to 0.29), lower potency 0.09 (-0.12 to 0.28). Relapse within 2 years of onset in a UK cohort of 256 patients (rated fair): 58% of those who used higher-potency cannabis daily against 24% of those who had used cannabis in the past (adjusted odds ratio 3.28, 1.22 to 9.18), lower-potency or infrequent higher-potency use 1.82 (0.36 to 8.75), adjusted for alcohol, other illicit drugs, cigarettes, care intensity at onset and medication adherence. Cross-sectional, all rated poor: self-reported lifetime psychosis diagnosis in a 20-country online survey of 181,870, higher- against lower-potency herbal 1.28 (1.07 to 1.53), butane hash oil against lower-potency herbal 1.11 (0.85 to 1.46) and against higher-potency herbal 0.89 (0.69 to 1.09); psychosis symptoms in 156 US adults, concentrates r 0.11 (-0.20 to 0.40), higher-potency herbal -0.27 (-0.45 to -0.06); residual or late-onset psychotic disorder in 71 Japanese patients, liquid or resin against dry herbal 0.212 (0.061 to 0.735).

Psychosis-like experiences: in a within-person comparison of 574 US adults who used cannabis in the past year, mostly infrequently, means were 1.2 when using herbal cannabis and 1.1 when using concentrates on a 0 to 10 scale (Cohen's d 0.12; rated poor); in a UK sample of 1,087 aged about 24, higher- against lower-potency use 1.29 (0.67 to 2.50) after adjustment for frequency, sex, childhood socio-economic position and psychotic experiences at 12 (rated fair).

Six cross-sectional studies of cannabis use disorder, one rated fair and five poor, with limits in the exposure measure in all six and in outcome measures, sample selection and confounder adjustment in the poor ones. Outcomes: Severity of Dependence Scale (two online surveys; 0 to 15, cut-off 3 or more), Cannabis Abuse Screening Test (UK sample of 1,087), MINI cannabis screening test (US sample of 191), a self-report questionnaire (US sample of 156) and an ICD-10 clinical interview (71 Japanese patients).

Four studies found more cannabis use disorder signs with higher potency. UK online survey 2009-10 (2,514; skunk against grass and resin; adjusted for gender and age; poor): each extra day a month of higher-potency use went with a Severity of Dependence Scale score 0.254 higher (0.161 to 0.357), with no association for grass (0.020, -0.029 to 0.070) or resin (0.025, -0.019 to 0.067). Survey of 55,240 people in 175 countries 2017-18 (adjusted for age, gender, amount and frequency of use and tobacco added; poor): classes using sinsemilla and herbal, b 0.155 (0.100 to 0.209), and hashish and herbal, b 0.262 (0.188 to 0.337), against herbal only. UK sample of 1,087 aged about 24 (Cannabis Abuse Screening Test; adjusted for sex, childhood socio-economic position, age at first use and frequency; fair): recent cannabis problems, odds ratio 4.08 (1.41 to 11.81). 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders (ICD-10 interview; no adjustment listed; poor): liquid or resin against dry herbal cannabis, dependence syndrome 6.850 (1.866 to 25.145).
key_findings.note: The text gives 6.9 (1.19 to 25.15) for the Japanese study and 0.161 to 0.3578 for the UK survey; Table 2 values are used here.

key_findings.finding: Two studies found no clear difference. US sample of 156 (self-report questionnaire; no adjustment listed; poor): higher-potency herbal use and symptoms of cannabis use disorder r 0.09 (-0.12 to 0.30); for concentrates the review prints -0.05 (-0.35 to -0.26) and the text reads it as fewer symptoms. US sample of 191 (MINI cannabis screening test; no adjustment listed; poor): people who frequently used concentrates did not endorse significantly more symptoms than people who frequently used herbal cannabis (means 2.1 and 1.3); the review notes that the sample endorsed few symptoms overall.
key_findings.note: The printed interval for the concentrate estimate does not contain the estimate; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Anxiety, four cross-sectional studies (one fair): generalised anxiety disorder in the UK sample of 1,087, higher- against lower-potency use 1.92 (1.11 to 3.32), adjusted for sex, childhood socio-economic position, depression score at 13 and frequency; in the 20-country survey, self-reported anxiety diagnosis with butane hash oil against lower-potency herbal 1.80 (1.60 to 2.01) and against higher-potency herbal 1.72 (1.55 to 1.91), higher- against lower-potency herbal 1.05 (0.98 to 1.12); no association in 156 US adults (concentrates r 0.21, -0.10 to 0.49; higher-potency herbal 0.03, -0.18 to 0.24) and no difference between frequent concentrate and frequent herbal use in 191 (means 1.1 and 0.66). Four studies of people using medical cannabis (one fair) gave varied results, some without intervals or statistical tests.

Depression, four cross-sectional studies (one fair): in the 20-country survey, self-reported depression diagnosis with higher- against lower-potency herbal 1.18 (1.11 to 1.25), butane hash oil against lower-potency herbal 1.34 (1.21 to 1.48) and against higher-potency herbal 1.15 (1.03 to 1.25); major depression in the UK sample of 1,087, 1.28 (0.68 to 2.32); no difference in the US sample of 191 (means 0.72 and 0.76) and no association in the US sample of 156 (concentrates r 0.17, -0.15 to 0.45; higher-potency herbal 0.02, -0.19 to 0.23). Three studies of people using medical cannabis (all poor) found greater relief with higher THC in one, the greatest reduction with the lowest THC in another, and differences not tested in the third.

The authors conclude that higher-potency use is associated with an increased risk of psychosis, higher in people who use daily, and with earlier onset, more symptoms and relapse; that the evidence does not suggest an association with psychosis-like symptoms; that higher potency was consistently associated with an increased risk of cannabis use disorder, recent problems and dependence severity, citing animal self-administration studies and a link between rising potency and treatment entry; and that there is some evidence for anxiety and little for depression.

Limits stated by the authors: most studies used self-reported product type, an approximate proxy for THC content; studies did not account for THC intake as opposed to content, which can differ through titration, which they say evidence suggests is partial and would be expected to weaken rather than inflate associations; dichotomous potency categories; some studies compared higher with lower potency directly and others each with no use, so results can be read only within each study; no meta-analysis was possible; cross-sectional designs cannot establish direction (people with poorer mental health might choose stronger cannabis as self-medication); there is no agreement on confounders, amount used was adjusted for in only one study, and frequency may be a confounder or a mediator. Other cannabinoids such as cannabidiol were not considered.
The Conclusion draws recommendations for education tools, clinical management and regulation by THC concentration (limits or taxes) from these findings; no certainty rating of the evidence is given.

Funding: ESRC South West Doctoral Training Partnership studentship (KP); Cancer Research UK fellowship C56067/A21330 and project award PPRCPJT\100023 (GT); Wellcome Trust 209158/Z/17/Z (LH); the funder had no role. Interests: GT reports previous funding from Pfizer (GRANT scheme) and owns a scientific consulting company doing unrelated work; the other authors declare none. The reference list shows the senior author as an author of at least five included studies and another review author as first author of one.
key_findings.locator: Contributors; Declaration of interests; Acknowledgments (p. 749); references 14, 15, 22, 27 and 30 (pp. 749-750)

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give 20 studies with 119,581 participants, but one included survey alone has 181,870 participants (Tables 1, 3 and 4), and the samples printed in Tables 1 to 4 sum to about 249,000 across the 16 distinct studies (editors' arithmetic, counting each study once).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed participant total cannot be used; any claim should give the samples of the individual studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The headline count of 20 'studies' counts articles: the GAP study appears in four articles and EU-GEI in two, so the tables hold 16 distinct studies (editors' count), while the per-outcome counts (8, 8, 7, 6) count each of GAP and EU-GEI once.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims must not count the GAP or EU-GEI articles as separate studies.

reporting_issues.issue: For the Japanese patients, the text gives dependence syndrome odds ratio 6.9 (95% CI 1.19 to 25.15) and Table 2 gives 6.850 (1.866 to 25.145).
reporting_issues.consequence: The lower limit differs; the table value is used, and the study is small (71) with no adjustment listed either way.

reporting_issues.issue: For concentrates in the US sample of 156, the review prints r -0.05 with 95% CI -0.35 to -0.26 (text and Table 2), an interval that does not contain its own estimate, and the text reads it as concentrate use associated with fewer symptoms of cannabis use disorder.
reporting_issues.consequence: The upper limit is probably a sign error (0.26); read as no association, as for the herbal estimate in the same study. Not checked against the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Signs differ between text and tables: the text prints the herbal anxiety estimate in the US sample of 156 as 0.03 (-0.18 to -0.24) and Table 3 as 0.03 (-0.18 to 0.24); the herbal depression estimate as 0.02 (0.19 to 0.23) in the text and 0.02 (-0.19 to 0.23) in Table 4; the medical cannabis anxiety coefficients (Stith 2020) as b 0.618 and 0.599 in the text and -0.618 and -0.599 in Table 3. The text also gives that US sample as 151 people for depression, against 156 in Table 4.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the table values; the substantive reading (no association; symptom relief) is unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 labels the Japanese chronic psychosis result 'No association' although its odds ratio 0.212 (0.061 to 0.735) excludes 1; the text describes fewer residual and late-onset psychotic disorders with higher potency.
reporting_issues.consequence: The estimate is an inverse association in a small clinical sample; the table label understates it.

reporting_issues.issue: The EU-GEI positive-symptom estimate is labelled an unstandardised coefficient b in Table 1 and a standardised coefficient beta in the text (0.22, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.29, an interval asymmetric around its estimate); the GAP odds ratio 2.91 (1.52 to 3.60) and the EU-GEI daily-use odds ratio 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3) sit near the upper ends of their intervals on the ratio scale.
reporting_issues.consequence: Possible misprints carried from or into the review; the primary papers were not read, so these figures are quoted as the review prints them.

reporting_issues.issue: In one medical cannabis study (Wan 2017) Table 3 lists the strength bands compared as 25-28%, 20-23% and 0.1-0.8% THC, while its findings column and text report 21-24%, 25-28% and 15-18%; the text cites table 4 for the quality ratings of the medical anxiety studies, which are in Table 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the medical cannabis findings are not used for claims.
